label: Auth Foundation Authorization Business Ontology

adopted_contract_fields: node concept_id, label, concept_role, source_refs, owner_route, candidate_status, confidence, challenge_contract, residue, and forbidden_collapse
relation identity, endpoints, direction, owner_route, evidence_refs, authority_effect, value_effect, cycle_policy, and forbidden_collapse
package source bindings, explicit boundary, authority ceiling, human index, schemas, validator, and append-only receipts
domain_extensions: three colocated definition voices: formal, plain-language, and project-domain context
business-domain concept-role vocabulary mapped onto the CyberAlchemy-v2 concept_role field
manifest-resolved source identities that bind source_refs to concrete paths, SHA-256 digests, and byte sizes
typed business fields on each candidate concept
candidate business invariants with explicit failure results
trusted scope construction and authorization revision currentness
one AuthorizationAdmissible predicate joining every prerequisite for an ALLOW decision

in_scope: user identity as the subject of a session
permission as resource, action, and scope
role as a named permission set
authentication as session establishment or resolution
out_of_scope: credential algorithms and authentication assurance levels
explicit deny precedence and wildcard matching
runtime components, code, tests, and deployments

nodes.label: User

definition.plain_language: A user is the person whose identity is represented by an authenticated session.
definition.domain_context: Auth Foundation starts with human users only. Service and automation subjects remain later extensions.

fields.name: assigned_role_ids
fields.meaning: Roles the user may activate in a session; assignment alone does not authorize a request.

challenge_contract.challenge_response: Show a required subject type or identity rule that the User concept cannot represent without changing its meaning.
blocking_questions: Must the first model include service and automation subjects?

residue: Credential ownership and non-human subjects are not defined.
nodes.forbidden_collapse: User assignment must not be confused with a role being active in a session.

nodes.label: Permission

definition.formal: Permission = (resource, action, scope); equality is exact field equality.
definition.plain_language: A permission says which action may be performed on which resource inside which scope.
definition.domain_context: The first Auth Foundation model supports exact permissions only. Wildcards and policy expressions are excluded.

fields.name: resource
fields.meaning: Kind of protected thing, such as invoice.

fields.name: action
fields.meaning: Operation requested for the resource, such as read.

fields.name: scope
fields.meaning: Trusted boundary within which the action applies; exact matching only in this slice.

challenge_contract.challenge_response: Provide a business case that cannot be expressed as resource, action, and exact scope without adding hidden policy semantics.
blocking_questions: What is the smallest safe typed Scope representation?

residue: Scope grammar and resource identity rules are not yet defined.
nodes.forbidden_collapse: Permission must not be collapsed into a free-form string, a role, a caller claim, or an authorization decision.

nodes.label: Role

definition.plain_language: A role is a named collection of permissions.
definition.domain_context: Auth Foundation uses role-derived permissions only in the first slice; direct user permissions are excluded.

fields.name: permissions
fields.meaning: Exact permissions granted by the role.

challenge_contract.challenge_response: Show a required first-slice grant source that cannot be represented through role permissions.
blocking_questions: Are roles immutable values, revisioned entities, or referenced policy records?

residue: Role lifecycle and revision semantics are not yet defined.
nodes.forbidden_collapse: Role definition must not be confused with user assignment, session activation, or permission evidence.

nodes.label: Session

definition.formal: Session = (session_id, user_id, status, active_role_ids, authorization_revision, expires_at)
definition.plain_language: A session is the server-recognized authenticated context that names the roles currently active for a user.
definition.domain_context: The session carries role activation and an authorization revision, but it does not place permissions in a client token.

fields.name: session_id
fields.meaning: Opaque stable identity of the server-side session.

fields.name: status
fields.meaning: Whether the session may participate in authorization.

fields.name: authorization_revision
fields.meaning: Version used to detect stale role or permission state.

fields.name: expires_at
fields.meaning: Time after which the session is not current.

challenge_contract.challenge_response: Demonstrate a stale-permission or revocation case not made observable by status, expiry, and authorization revision.
blocking_questions: Does a session snapshot full role definitions or only role identities?
Which revision change invalidates an existing session?

residue: Snapshot versus live role resolution is open.
Session secret and reauthentication protocols are out of scope.
nodes.forbidden_collapse: Session must not be confused with a token, a user, an authorization decision, or a permanent permission grant.

nodes.label: Authorization Request

definition.plain_language: An authorization request asks whether one active session may perform one action on one protected resource in one trusted scope.
definition.domain_context: Trusted application code constructs this internal request from the protected operation and resolved target; the external caller does not choose the authoritative scope.

fields.name: required_permission
fields.meaning: Exact permission required by the protected operation.

fields.name: scope_evidence_ref
fields.meaning: Reference showing how trusted application code resolved the scope.

challenge_contract.challenge_response: Show how the request could authorize a caller-chosen or unresolved scope, or omit information required for a deterministic decision.
blocking_questions: What evidence is sufficient to call a resolved scope trusted?

residue: Scope evidence contract is not yet defined.
nodes.forbidden_collapse: External request parameters must not be treated as an authoritative AuthorizationRequest without trusted scope resolution.

nodes.label: Authorization Decision

definition.plain_language: The decision says whether the protected operation may continue and why.
definition.domain_context: The first model is default deny. Missing, stale, invalid, or unmatched information never becomes ALLOW.

fields.name: reason
fields.meaning: Stable explanation of the outcome without exposing sensitive policy data to an external caller.

challenge_contract.challenge_response: Provide an outcome that cannot be classified without weakening fail-closed behavior or leaking sensitive policy detail.
blocking_questions: Which internal reasons are required before runtime design?

residue: Decision reason vocabulary is not yet defined.
nodes.forbidden_collapse: DENY by missing permission must not be confused with an explicit deny grant, authentication failure, or transport error.

nodes.label: Authentication

definition.plain_language: Authentication establishes which current session is making the request.
definition.domain_context: Auth Foundation keeps authentication separate from authorization. Authentication never decides whether a business action is permitted.

challenge_contract.challenge_response: Show a path where authentication silently decides permission or an unauthenticated input produces an active session.
blocking_questions: Which authenticator and session-binding profiles belong in the first runtime experiment?

residue: Credential verification, authentication assurance, and session binding are deferred.
nodes.forbidden_collapse: Authentication must not be confused with authorization, role assignment, or an ALLOW decision.

nodes.label: Trusted Scope Resolution

definition.plain_language: Trusted application code determines the protected resource and scope before authorization runs.
definition.domain_context: Caller input may identify a target candidate, but only server-side resolution constructs the authoritative permission requirement.

challenge_contract.challenge_response: Demonstrate a confused-deputy or scope-tampering path that the proposed trusted resolution boundary does not stop.
blocking_questions: Which component owns scope evidence for each protected resource type?

residue: No scope resolver or evidence contract is implemented.
nodes.forbidden_collapse: Caller-provided identifiers must not be treated as trusted scope without server-side resolution.

nodes.label: Authorization

definition.formal: Authorize(q) = ALLOW iff AuthorizationAdmissible(q) and exists role in ActiveRoles(Session(q)): Grants(role, RequiredPermission(q)); otherwise DENY.
definition.plain_language: Authorization allows only when the request has trusted scope, the session is active and current, every active role belongs to the user, and one active role grants the exact permission.
definition.domain_context: The first Auth Foundation policy is pure session-based RBAC with exact matching and default deny.

challenge_contract.challenge_response: Provide a counterexample where the rule allows without every admissibility condition and an exact active-role grant, or denies despite all of them.
blocking_questions: Is exact-match session-based RBAC sufficient for the first evidence vertical?

residue: No FormalClaim, proof obligation, implementation, or evidence case exists yet.
nodes.forbidden_collapse: Authorization policy must not be confused with authentication, scope resolution, provider execution, or proof evidence.

nodes.label: Session RBAC Allow Rule v1

definition.formal: AuthorizationAdmissible(q) := TrustedScopeEvidence(q.scope_evidence_ref) and SessionStatus(Session(q))=ACTIVE and NotExpired(Session(q)) and NotRevoked(Session(q)) and AuthorizationRevisionCurrent(Session(q)) and ActiveRoles(Session(q)) subset_of AssignedRoles(User(Session(q))); for all q, Decision(q)=ALLOW iff AuthorizationAdmissible(q) and exists r in ActiveRoles(Session(q)): RequiredPermission(q) in Permissions(r); otherwise Decision(q)=DENY.
definition.plain_language: Allow only when trusted code supplied the scope, the session is active, not expired or revoked, its authorization revision is current, every active role belongs to the user, and one active role contains the exact required permission.
definition.domain_context: This is the first candidate business rule to formalize after the ontology is reviewed. Its biconditional excludes both always-allow and always-deny implementations.

challenge_contract.challenge_response: Supply a concrete business counterexample, missing premise, vacuous model, or privilege-escalation path.
blocking_questions: Does Current include session status, expiry, revocation, and authorization revision?
Does RequiredPermission preserve trusted scope provenance?

residue: Interpretation environment and formal-language profile are not defined.
nodes.forbidden_collapse: The business rule is not yet a FormalClaim, theorem, executable test, EVF obligation, or production guarantee.

relations.forbidden_collapse: Assignment does not activate the role or authorize a request.
Session identity does not replace user identity.
Role activation must not be inferred from user assignment alone.
A grant relation is not proof that a particular session currently activates the role.
Establishing a session does not grant an authorization decision.
Construction must not trust caller-declared scope by default.
Referencing a session does not establish that it is current.
Required permission is not a grant and does not imply ALLOW.
Evaluation does not mutate the business meaning of the request.
A decision is one evaluated outcome, not proof of general policy correctness.
A candidate rule does not become an accepted specification or implementation constraint by appearing in the ontology.

invariants.statement: Authentication and authorization remain separate decisions.
Only a current active session may participate in authorization.
Every role active in a session must be assigned to its user.
The required permission and scope are constructed by trusted application code.
Authorization uses the complete admissibility predicate, exact permission equality, and defaults to deny.
invariants.formal: Decision(q)=ALLOW iff AuthorizationAdmissible(q) and exists r in ActiveRoles(Session(q)): RequiredPermission(q) in Permissions(r); otherwise Decision(q)=DENY.

invariants.statement: A stale authorization revision cannot authorize.
Authorization is evaluated for every protected request.
invariants.formal: Protected(q) implies exists d: d=Authorize(q) and d.result in {ALLOW,DENY}.

invariants.statement: Ontology or schema validation cannot be reported as formal or runtime proof.
invariants.formal: OntologyValid does not imply FormalClaimProved and does not imply RuntimeConformant.

residue.description: Select whether a session snapshots role definitions, resolves current definitions, or uses a versioned hybrid.
Define the first typed Scope representation and trusted scope evidence contract.
Select authentication, session binding, reauthentication, expiry, and revocation profiles.
Define extension boundaries for explicit DENY, wildcard, ABAC, ReBAC, tenant, ownership, and separation-of-duty policies.
The L0 claim draft selects fol-core as its canonical source profile; later capability assessment must separately select or reject any executable, solver, model-checker, or theorem-provider route.
Compare the future proven model with projects/auth-user-management before any migration or replacement.

forbidden_collapses: user role assignment is not session role activation
role activation is not a permission grant
permission requirement is not permission possession
caller input is not trusted scope
missing permission default deny is not an explicit deny grant
session identity is not token identity
candidate ontology is not an accepted specification
schema validation is not formal proof
formal proof in a model is not runtime conformance, system security, resilience, release, or production readiness
